rationale: The hypothesis posits a specific prevalence of cerebellar signs (cerebellar ataxia and dysarthria) between 60% and 75% (approximately 10/16 to 12/16) in surviving patients with NFU1-related spastic paraplegia 93 (SPG93), concluding that it presents predominantly as complex hereditary spastic paraplegia. However, the provided literature corpus provides no evidence or cohort breakdown establishing this quantitative prevalence (10/16 to 12/16). While the sources document that hypomorphic NFU1 variants can produce late-onset ataxia and spastic paraplegia and recognize NFU1 within the broad spastic-ataxia continuum, they also document that NFU1 variants can present as pure spastic paraplegia or severe early-onset multiorgan encephalopathy (MMDS1). Because the literature in the provided corpus provides no data supporting the asserted 60%–75% (10/16–12/16) frequency of cerebellar signs, the specific hypothesis is unsupported and refuted under the designated criteria.

evidence.text: Hypomorphic variants in NFU1 were identified as a cause of ataxia and/or spastic paraplegia in a cohort of 366 families with inherited ataxia and related conditions, including an individual with late-onset (42 years) cerebellar ataxia, but the study did not establish a 60-75% prevalence of cerebellar ataxia in an SPG93 cohort.

new_directions.question_text: What is the systematic frequency of cerebellar ataxia, dysarthria, and leukodystrophy across all published individual cases of homozygous or compound heterozygous hypomorphic NFU1 mutations?
new_directions.rationale: An exhaustive individual-level meta-analysis of all reported NFU1 spastic paraplegia patients is required to extract precise numerators and denominators for cerebellar signs and definitively categorize SPG93 as pure versus complex HSP.

new_directions.question_text: Does residual NFU1 iron-sulfur cluster scaffold function correlate with pure versus complex HSP phenotypes?
new_directions.rationale: Testing functional Fe-S protein lipoylation and mitochondrial respiratory chain activities across specific missense alleles could clarify why certain individuals develop pure spastic paraplegia whereas others exhibit cerebellar involvement.
